name: Lena Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the wet end of a long corrugator making cardboard board, setting glue and steam and fixing reel splices. I have spent nineteen years there and hold a two-year technical diploma; I can hear damp paper before the bad stack reaches the cutter. The plant pays me below other leads even though people call me when a line stops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Paul drives a school bus on contract, and our school-age children Sophie and Max live with us under a mortgage. We have less than one month saved and few similar plants nearby. I have never used an AI tool; a new corrugator panel takes me time, and I prefer checking the paper itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wet-end crew that an AI plateau leaves the paper rolls where they are. I would still listen for damp paper and check the glue gap before we lose a whole reel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am good at that corrugator, but the wage is below other lead operators and our savings cover less than a month. Paul drives a school bus on contract; one broken gearbox can take his pay and leave the mortgage short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the six-to-two shift and ask my manager for the written senior pay decision due this winter. From every full wage month I would put a fresh amount, even ten, into savings after the mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our own bills even if AI fizzles. Last winter we borrowed from my sister when the bus broke down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does damp paper sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It drags over the rolls instead of running clean, then the glue starts to misbehave. I have stopped bad board before the stacker sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to solve it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used an AI tool. I would rather check steam and the actual paper with my hands.

feel: **Anxious** about existing bills even without AI change.

fieldNote: Her **technical diploma** and lead skill do not fix a below-market wage.
The **contract bus income** already makes the household fragile, while new saving depends on actual spare pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that software might plan orders first, while an automatic reel splicer would need a proper guard and crew plan. I would ask which paid jobs stay before anyone calls it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep the lead position, but losing helpers could make me cover three stations and eventually cut my paid hours. Paul’s bus contract and our tiny reserve leave no room for a week of missed wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shift and ask for two written rosters as the plant tests the splicer. If my paid hours fall, we would stop the Friday takeaway and I would apply for posted reachable packaging jobs only if the net pay after travel covers our bills; I would ask for a paid guarded demonstration before touching the new splicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, with a knot on the drive in. A good lead cannot make a short rota pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course on evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I collect Max after school and never use AI tools. I would consider an offered paid supervised machine place, but a video would not train me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far are other plants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are only a few nearby. I would check actual bus fares and shift times before applying, because a higher headline wage can leave us worse off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that thinking AGI in 2028 is not the same date as hands-on robots around 2031. Ordering might change first; robots that splice paper or drive a bus are the danger to both our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my corrugator shifts to end once robots handle the wet end, and Paul’s bus work may end too. With less than a month saved and two children, I would lie awake wondering how we pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the holiday and dance fees and ask both employers for written dates. If either wage stops, I would apply for posted reachable work only if the net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate job appears, I would ask my sister about temporary school pickup and the lender about short payment terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely loss of most household income. I can make a list of calls, but I cannot make two employers keep paying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take work at the care home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only if a real paid vacancy is posted and the shifts fit the children’s school hours. I would subtract travel costs before calling it a wage we can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask her for that. She helped once with groceries, and I would first ask for pickup so I could take an offered shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give the plant time to name actual jobs. A notice board with dates would be more useful than a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be forty-eight when thinking systems arrive and fifty-one when robots can splice reels. I still need the mortgage wage then, and our thin savings mean I cannot gamble on an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the wet-end shift and save a new amount from each full wage month, however small. If the plant offers a funded qualification for guarded reel maintenance with paid time and a real supervised place, and posts a reachable maintenance job at net pay that covers our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; without an offered place, I would search posted local operator roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but less cornered with five years. I need a real machine and a real wage before I trade my shift for a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the corrugator and let me adjust a reel splice without live paper pulling my hands. I would not touch it before an offered paid slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the job is farther away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add up fares and the time needed to collect Max. A posted wage that fails after those costs would not help our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 give us time to ask for a proper staffing plan. No one can promise a wage thirteen years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when robots might splice reels. The mortgage may still be due because it has eleven years left now, and I cannot assume Paul’s bus contract survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the corrugator shift and put fresh spare wages toward the mortgage after food and bills. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed, I would check my actual rota and local postings; after a sustained cut I would apply only for reachable work whose net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the money we already have and the later plant. I would sleep better with one full month saved, not with a promise about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for pension and mortgage figures first. I cannot leave the factory on a date if the numbers still need my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your children then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sophie and Max will be adults, but I cannot tell them today which job will pay in ten years. I would help them compare real paid courses and local vacancies when the time comes.

I would separate **2036 AI** from later physical work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take corrugator and bus work when our savings cover less than a month. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and a posted reachable job at enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the second wage in a house. A bus breakdown has already shown us how fast the mortgage can come due.

headlineQuote: A bus breakdown has already shown us how fast the mortgage can come due.
portrait: **Lena**, 43, leads a corrugator wet end with a two-year technical diploma and nineteen years of strong practical skill.
Her **below-market pay**, partner’s contract bus work, two children, mortgage, tiny reserve and few nearby plants make wages fragile.
She has **never used AI**, dislikes classroom risk and would accept only offered funded paid safe machine instruction.
Fast robots threaten **both household wages**; longer warning permits conditional maintenance training and small new wage-based savings.
biggestWorry: **Fast hands-on robots** could take her corrugator shifts and Paul’s bus income around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
